Oliveyards
OL-iv-yardz
noun (plural)
From olive, Latin oliva, joined to yard, the Saxon geard, an enclosure; hence the walled or hedged plantation of olive trees. It renders the Hebrew zayith in the collective, the olive-ground of a family’s inheritance.

Biblical Definition

An oliveyard is an enclosed plantation of olive trees — slow-growing, long-lived, and the steadiest wealth a family in Canaan could hold, since the tree gives oil for food, for light, for anointing and for the sanctuary, and gives it for generations. Its doctrinal weight lies in a single clause Joshua repeats to the assembled tribes: “I have given you a land for which ye did not labour, and cities which ye built not, and ye dwell in them; of the vineyards and oliveyards which ye planted not do ye eat” (Jos 24:13). Moses had prepared them for the same mercy and warned of its danger — houses they filled not, wells they digged not, olive trees they planted not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full, beware lest thou forget the LORD (Deu 6:11–12). This is unearned inheritance, covenant grace in the shape of trees planted by other men’s hands, and it is the closest thing in the Old Testament to a parable of justification: a people put in possession of a fruitfulness they did not produce. Two dark uses answer it. Samuel warns that the king they demand will take their oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants (1Sa 8:14). And Elisha, seeing through Gehazi’s lie about Naaman’s silver, asks the question that exposes the heart: “Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards?” (2Ki 5:26). Grace freely given may be neither stolen by a king nor bargained for by a prophet’s servant.

Webster 1828 Definition

An enclosed plantation of olive trees; in Scripture the emblem of inheritance received without labour — covenant grace in the form of trees Israel never planted.

expand to see more

OLIVEYARD, n. [Olive and yard, Saxon geard, an enclosure.] An enclosure or piece of ground in which olives are cultivated.

The olive yields oil for food, for lamps, for anointing, and for the offerings of the sanctuary.

Being slow of growth and long of life, it represents settled and inherited estate.

Named with vineyards in the lists of what Israel received but did not plant (Jos 24:13; Neh 9:25).

Taken away by kings (1Sa 8:14) and restored by repentant rulers (Neh 5:11).

Key Scripture

Jos 24:13 — "And I have given you a land for which ye did not labour, and cities which ye built not, and ye dwell in them; of the vineyards and oliveyards which ye planted not do ye eat."

Deu 6:11 — "And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;"

2Ki 5:26 — "And he said unto him, Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants?"

Neh 5:11 — "Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them."

Modern Corruption

Unearned inheritance is read as a lesson in gratitude only, with the doctrine beneath it — that God gives what we did not labour for — softened into the notion that Israel earned Canaan by conquest and obedience.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is nearer home: the quiet assumption that what we hold, we produced. Joshua’s sentence forbids it in the sharpest possible terms — a land ye laboured not for, cities ye built not, oliveyards ye planted not. Israel did fight, and fought hard; but the fighting did not create the olive trees, and Moses had already told them the reason for the gift was not their righteousness, for they were a stiffnecked people (Deu 9:6). This is the shape of grace, and it is the shape of the believer’s whole estate: a righteousness he did not work out, a peace he did not make, a place at a table he did not set. The man who forgets it will do one of two things — boast, or grasp after more. Deu 6:12 names the danger exactly: when thou shalt have eaten and be full, beware lest thou forget the LORD which brought thee forth.

Recover the gratitude and the guard together. Gehazi is the warning for the ministry: a servant of the prophet who saw free grace given to a Syrian and calculated what he could extract from it — oliveyards and vineyards, sheep and oxen — and carried away Naaman’s leprosy with the silver. Samuel is the warning for the state: what a family received as inheritance, a king will take “even the best of them” and hand to his courtiers, which is why the landmark law and the jubilee stood guard over Israel’s fields. And Nehemiah is the pattern of repentance: restore, this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards. Grace received freely makes a man generous, not acquisitive.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Enclosed olive plantations; the trees Israel did not plant, standing for an inheritance wholly of grace.

expand to see more

Oliveyard — olive (Latin oliva) + yard (Saxon geard, an enclosure).

Hebrew zayith, the olive tree and its ground; oil for food, light, anointing and offering.

Jos 24:13 and Deu 6:11 — the unlaboured inheritance, with its warning against forgetting.

1Sa 8:14 — the king will take your oliveyards, even the best of them.

2Ki 5:26 and Neh 5:11 — grasped after by Gehazi, restored by Nehemiah’s reform.

Usage

"The clause to press is “which ye planted not” — the whole doctrine sits there."

"Olive trees outlive their planters, which is why they figure inheritance rather than harvest."

"Gehazi’s oliveyards show grace turned into a commodity by a man close to the prophet."
